//physical: What the board *is*, physically. The PCB design needs the footprint and the outline; the simulator needs a size to place parts around. Every number here is from DFRobot's own dimension drawing V1.3 (and their board render, for the silkscreen order), parsed geometrically rather than read off a picture.

physical.//footprint: Generated by tools/generate-firebeetle-footprint.py, not downloaded. Published footprints for this board disagree: the row spacing is 22.86 mm (the through-holes), not 25.40 mm (the castellated half-holes on the edge), and at least one public KiCad footprint uses the latter, which will not mate.

header.//drill_mm: DFRobot's own finished hole for DFRobot's own obround pad. It is NOT the hole to put in a board this module plugs into: a 2.54 mm header pin is 0.64 mm square, so 0.905 mm across the diagonal, and a 0.9 mm drill finishes near 0.84 mm after plating. Carried because it is what the vendor drawing says; emit_footprint.py deliberately ignores it and sizes the hole from the pin that has to go in.
header.//alignment: Both rows are flush at the end away from USB-C; the 18-pin row runs four pitches further toward the USB end.
header.//first_pad_from_edge_mm: Centre of the first pad of BOTH rows, from the flush edge. This was prose inside the line above until 2026-09-25, which meant the one number tying the pads to the outline could not be read by anything - the same defect as the header order itself. Check: 60.0/2 - 5.2 = 24.80 mm, where the hand-checked footprint puts pad 1.

physical.//max_component_height: NOT stated by DFRobot for this board. The STEP model suggests ~7 mm above the top face, but it includes the camera and its FPC and could not be reduced to board-only, so no number is recorded here rather than a guessed one.
physical.//header_order: Which silkscreen label sits on which PAD, per row, in physical order from the flush end. The geometry above is precise to 0.01 mm and this is the one fact that cannot be derived from it — a cold rebuild of this board was blocked here, and had to guess. UNRESOLVED: pads 14 and 16 of the 18-pin row. This file calls them GND1/GND3 from one reading of DFRobot's schematic; a later reading of the same schematic and the board photo says they are silkscreened NC and carry no net. Treating them as GND is the safe direction — a ground trace terminating on an unconnected pad is harmless, whereas treating a real ground pad as NC loses a return path. Settle it with a continuity meter, module to pad.

header_order.//: 18-pin row first, then the 14-pin row; each from the end away from the USB-C.

physical.//pad_aliases: Where a pin's NAME in `pins` differs from the label silkscreened on its PAD. The silkscreen abbreviates, and one GPIO is brought out twice. A footprint generated from the silkscreen gives a pad called MI while the design writes a trace to MISO, and they do not connect — silently, because nothing downstream knows the two words mean one pad.

//wokwi_part_type: Wokwi has no FireBeetle 2 S3 part (wokwi/wokwi-boards lists no such board), so the simulation stands in the generic S3 devkit. This is honest rather than approximate: it is the same silicon, it exposes GPIO 0-21 and 35-48 - a superset of every pin this board brings out - and it names its pins by raw GPIO number, which is what the diagram generator emits anyway. What is lost is the silkscreen labels in the simulator picture, and nothing else.
//wokwi_pin_naming: Wokwi's stand-in part (the generic S3 devkit) names its pins by raw GPIO number - "12", "13" - not by this board's silkscreen. Its power pins are suffixed: 3V3.1, GND.1.
//power_pads: Which pad carries which rail, and which way it flows. This fact existed only as `wokwi_power_pins` until 2026-09-25 - the same knowledge, named for one consumer, so the schematic generator could not read it and emitted no power connection for the module at all. The generated board's microcontroller shared a net with NONE of its 32 pins: no ground, no 3.3 V. It built, routed 8 of 11 traces, and the gate called it done. VCC was deliberately absent until 2026-09-30 (P29), on the argument that it is the USB 5 V rail, an output these designs do not consume, and that wiring it up by default is how 5 V reaches 3.3 V logic. Half of that is right and the other half cost a board: the irrigation controller's buck record says in its own words 'Feeds the FireBeetle's 5 V/VCC input and the sensors', and the generated board had no such trace - net.V5V joined the buck to a flow meter and the processor was fed by nothing. So VCC is recorded here as `direction: in`, which the generator reads as CONDITIONAL: wired only when something else on the board drives that rail, and left alone - with the reason printed in the file - when nothing does. That is the dual role stated once, in the one place that knows it.

3V3.//can_supply: P52: the figures a rail's load is summed against. The module powers its own ESP32 from this regulator before anything on the header gets any, so its own draw is a load on the rail it supplies.

VCC.//feeds: P52: what reaches 3V3 comes in here, through a step-down converter, so this pad draws at most what 3V3 carries - an upper bound, the only one a record can give.
VCC.//: The 5 V input. DFRobot: '5 V DC for powering the board (cannot charge Li-ion battery)' - see power.feeding_vcc_charges_the_battery, verified. It is a pad that works both ways and only one of them is this board's business: with nothing on the rail it carries the USB 5 V OUT, which is why `direction: in` does not mean 'always wire it'. It reaches VSYS through a P-FET, not a short (power.vcc_is_not_tied_to_vsys), so the FET is the practical current ceiling and DFRobot rate neither.

//pins: The silkscreen label on the board, and the GPIO it actually is. This is the single most error-prone fact about any board: here D2 is GPIO3, D9 is GPIO0, and D13 is GPIO21. The labels are not a sequence and must never be inferred. Note that D0, D1, D4 and D8 do not exist on this board - DFRobot skips them.
//wake_capable_gpio: GPIO0-21, because SOC_RTCIO_PIN_COUNT is 22 on the S3. This is the headline difference from the XIAO ESP32-C6, where only GPIO0-7 could wake the chip and the whole pin map was bent around three usable pins. Here almost every header pin can wake it, so the pin map is free to be chosen for other reasons. The header pins that CANNOT wake it are D3 (38), D14 (47), TX (43) and RX (44).
//adc_gpio: ADC1 only - GPIO1-10. The S3 has a second ADC on GPIO11-20, but ADC2 shares hardware with the radio and cannot be read while WiFi is on, so it is deliberately not listed as usable. That is why A5 appears under pin_roles as a caveat rather than here: it is silkscreened as an analogue pin and is one, on the ADC you cannot use.
//pin_roles: What a pin IS, beyond its number. Typed so a program can read it: the arrays are for checks, the notes are for people. A pin with a role is not unusable - it is usable with a caveat, and the caveat is the note.

strapping.note: D9 is GPIO0, the BOOT pin - held low at reset it enters the bootloader, so nothing may drive it low during power-up. D2 is GPIO3, the JTAG source select strap. Both are usable as ordinary I/O once running; neither is safe for something that idles low.

adc2_unusable_with_wifi.note: on ADC2, which shares hardware with the radio. A5 (GPIO11) is the one that matters here: it is labelled analogue but cannot be read with WiFi active. Use A0-A4 or D5/D7 for analogue instead.

onboard_led.note: the on-board user LED, silkscreened D13. Usable, but it will blink whatever you put on it.

onboard_button.note: the on-board user button, silkscreened D14. Already has a button on it, and cannot wake the chip from deep sleep.

not_wake_capable.note: outside the RTC domain, so these cannot wake the chip however they are configured. Everything else on the header can.

console_uart.note: U0TXD and U0RXD — the ROM bootloader prints here on every reset and the serial console uses both. TX is driven push-pull at boot, so anything that acts on a level (a motor driver input, an enable line) twitches every time the board resets. Usable in a pinch, never a first choice, and taking them costs you the console you need during bring-up.

spi.note: MOSI, MISO, SCK and SS: the hardware SPI bus, silkscreened MO, MI, SCK and A4. A design with no SPI may use them — but they are taken LAST, because the assigner spent the whole bus on two LEDs and a button when nothing marked it, and a later SPI part then had nowhere to go. Recorded 2026-09-29 (backlog P3).

i2c.note: SDA and SCL: the hardware I2C bus. Same reasoning as spi. The smart bin never hit this only because its rangefinder claims both pins before anything else is placed.

//deep_sleep: How this chip is woken. Unlike the C6, the S3 has real RTC IO and defines SOC_PM_SUPPORT_EXT0_WAKEUP, so esp32.wake_on_ext0 exists - it takes a single pin at either polarity. What the S3 does NOT have is SOC_PM_SUPPORT_EXT1_WAKEUP_MODE_PER_PIN, which the C6 does: its ext1 applies one trigger level to every pin at once. So with two wake sources the shared-polarity constraint is back, for the opposite reason to the C6's.

deep_sleep.//simulated_by_wokwi: Established by experiment on the C6 - Wokwi wakes from a timer but not from a GPIO. Assumed to hold for the S3 stand-in; not retested.
deep_sleep.//polarity_is_a_wiring_decision: Which level wakes the chip is NOT a fact about this board - it follows from how the buttons are wired, so it lives in config.WAKE_ON_HIGH. What IS a fact about this board is the line above: one level applies to every ext1 pin at once, so every wake source must agree.
deep_sleep.//micropython_low_level_wake_bug: MicroPython #17334 (a pin stuck asserted after a low-level wake) is open upstream, reported on a C6 with v1.25.0. It has NOT been observed on any board in this project - nothing here has run on hardware - and whether it affects the S3 is untested. It is a reason to prefer waking on HIGH, not a measured fault. (Corrected 2026-10-01, P63: this note said it 'was hit on the C6' and quoted one project's config value, which had since changed.)

//wokwi_power_pins: Pads that are not GPIOs, so no naming rule covers them. Keyed by the name the footprint gives the pad, because that is what the emitter looks up. VCC was added 2026-09-30: P29 began wiring that pad on boards whose design drives a 5 V rail, and the simulation then stopped with 'VCC is not a pin of board-esp32-s3-devkitc-1' — the stand-in devkit calls the same pin 5V. A pad this board CAN wire must have a name in the simulator, or the design is unsimulable the first time somebody feeds it.
//vendor: Where the pin map can be RE-DERIVED from, so it is verified rather than trusted. tools/../check_vendor_pins.py fetches this header and compares.
//hardware_revisions: One SKU, two different power designs. A board file that states a fact true of only some boards carrying its SKU is asserting something with no stated scope, which is how a correct-looking number becomes wrong on someone else's desk.

hardware_revisions.source: DFRobot's wiki carries two Board Overview tabs, and the schematics zip carries both V1.0.0 and V1.3.0: https://dfimg.dfrobot.com/wiki/20529/DFR0975_firebeetle-esp32-s3-ai-acceleration-board_schematics_V1.3.zip
hardware_revisions.how_to_tell: Look at the chip between the BOOT button and the USB-C. A QFN marked AXP313A is V1.1 or earlier; a tiny SOT-563 next to two SOT-23-5 LDOs is V1.2 or later. The back silkscreen also carries the revision.

v1_1_and_earlier.3v3_regulator: AXP313A PMIC, DCDC1, 1.5 A (X-Powers datasheet, not DFRobot)
v1_1_and_earlier.i2c_pullups: 5.1k to 3V3 already present on SDA/SCL — they are the PMIC's own bus pull-ups, and the PMIC is another device on your I2C bus
v1_1_and_earlier.user_button: also drives the PMIC's PWRON through a diode, so a long press can power the board down and the pin reads ~0.7 V pressed, not 0 V

v1_2_and_later.3v3_regulator: TPS62A02 buck, 2 A (TI datasheet, not DFRobot)
v1_2_and_later.i2c_pullups: NONE anywhere on the board. Every I2C device must bring its own, or the bus does not work at all
v1_2_and_later.user_button: a plain button: 5.1k pull-up, 100 nF, switch to ground

//power: What DFRobot document, and what only the component datasheets say. DFRobot publish no current rating for either rail and no quiescent figure at all.

vcc_is_not_tied_to_vsys.note: VCC reaches VSYS through a SI2301 P-FET with a dual-PNP gate drive and a 6.2 V zener clamp. Functionally VCC follows VSYS, but it is a switch, not a short, and the FET is the practical current ceiling — DFRobot rate neither.

charge_current_a.source: DFRobot wiki 'Max Charging Current: 1A'; schematic V1.3.0 ETA6003 ISET1 = 1k
charge_current_a.note: Not settable in software or by a jumper — changing it means replacing R2. Battery temperature protection is disabled on this board: NTC is tied to ground.

feeding_vcc_charges_the_battery.source: DFRobot wiki: '5 V DC for powering the board (cannot charge Li-ion battery)'

regulator_3v3_a.source: hardware_revisions: the AXP313A's DCDC1 is 1.5 A (V1.1 and earlier), the TPS62A02 is 2 A (V1.2 and later) - the lower, because one record covers both. Both come from the chip makers' datasheets as cited there; neither was re-read at source for this field.
regulator_3v3_a.why_it_matters: What everything on 3V3 is summed against, the module's own radio included. DFRobot rate neither regulator.

module_peak_a.source: ESP32-S3-WROOM-1 datasheet v1.1, Table 11 (page 15): 802.11b, 1 Mbps, @20.5 dBm TX, 355 mA peak at 3.3 V.
module_peak_a.note: The radio's transmit peak, which is the most the module itself takes. With WiFi off it is far less; the sum uses the peak because a brown-out happens at the peak.

deep_sleep_ua.source: DFRobot publish no quiescent or deep-sleep figure for either SKU. Espressif's ESP32-S3-WROOM-1 datasheet v1.1, Table 12 (page 15): Deep-sleep 8 uA with RTC peripherals on, 7 uA with them off. Its footnote 1 - add 140 uA for 8 MB octal PSRAM (3.3 V) - is attached to the Light-sleep row, NOT to Deep-sleep; v1.8's Table 6-7 attaches it the same way
deep_sleep_ua.why_it_matters: Would decide which SKU to buy, and is unmeasured. This used to say the N16R8's PSRAM costs ~140 uA in deep sleep; the datasheet it cited attaches that figure to light sleep (corrected 2026-10-01, P63). Whether octal PSRAM draws anything in deep sleep is a bench measurement, and until it exists neither SKU is preferred on current.

io_volts.source: ESP32-S3-WROOM-1 datasheet v1.1, Table 9 (page 14): VDD33 power supply voltage 3.0 min, 3.3 typ, 3.6 max V. Table 10: VOH is at least 0.8 x VDD measured into a high-impedance load, and a pin sources 40 mA (typ) at VOH >= 2.64 V with PAD_DRIVER = 3 - so at an indicator's few milliamps a pin sits close to 3.3 V, and a resistor computed from 3.3 V gives at most the current asked for.
io_volts.why_it_matters: the voltage a GPIO drives, from which a series resistor's value is computed (P78)
